header.title: Applied Rate Modelling
header.subtitle: Density, flow, heartbeats, acceleration and the rate a fire spreads

meta.lesson-focus: Model applied rate contexts — density, birth rate, flow rate, heart rate; vehicle acceleration and deceleration; explore fire-spread rate techniques in First Nations Australians' land management under varying fuel types, wind, temperature and humidity.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving direct proportion, rates, ratio and scale, including financial contexts; formulate the problems and interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate the model and report methods and findings
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Mathematical modelling can be used to represent and solve problems involving proportion, rates, ratios and scale, including in financial contexts

html.section0_intro: Today's lesson builds on rates, unit conversion and direct proportion. These three questions check you are ready.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's maths. Estimate first: commit a gut answer before anyone calculates.

A smartwatch reports your resting heart rate: about 70 beats per minute. A car ad says 0 to 100 km/h in 8 seconds. A bushfire report gives the fire front's rate of spread in metres per minute.

Every one of these is a rate: one quantity per unit of another. Know the rate and you can predict: how many beats in a day, how fast after 3 seconds, how long until the fire reaches the track.

Today you formulate a rate from data, use it to predict, and evaluate whether the model is sensible. Units do the heavy lifting: a rate in km/h is not a rate in m/s until you convert it.
❤️ Your heart beats at a steady 70 beats per minute, all day and all night. Roughly how many times does it beat in one day? Pick a rung, then type your estimate. No calculator yet!
html.vocab_cards:
Rate
Tap to flip
Compares two quantities with different units: an amount per one unit of something else.
72 beats/min; 12 L/min; 30 m/min.
Density
Tap to flip
Mass per unit volume: density = mass ÷ volume.
Aluminium: 2.7 g/cm³, so 1 cm³ has a mass of 2.7 g.
Flow rate
Tap to flip
Volume per unit time: flow rate = volume ÷ time.
A hose filling 60 L in 2.5 min flows at 24 L/min.
Birth rate
Tap to flip
Births per year for every 1000 people in the population.
300 births in a town of 25 000 → 12 per 1000 per year.
Acceleration
Tap to flip
Change in velocity per second: a = (v − u) ÷ t, in m/s². Negative means slowing down (deceleration).
0 to 24 m/s in 8 s → 3 m/s².
html.section3_desc: Drag each quantity into ✓ A rate or ✗ Not a rate.
html.sort_activity:
Is it a rate?
Density of gold: 19.3 g/cm³ Map scale 1 : 50 000 Tap flow: 12 L/min Concrete mix 3 : 1 sand to cement Heart: 72 beats per minute Relative humidity 40% Car speeds up by 3 m/s every second Temperature 25 °C Fire front moves 30 m/min Room 4 m long and 3 m wide

✓ A rate (different units)

✗ Not a rate

💡 Test: does it say per (or /) with two different units? A ratio of the same units (1 : 50 000, 3 : 1), a percentage or a single measurement is not a rate. Humidity and temperature still affect a fire's rate of spread, but they are not rates themselves.

html.worked_example:
The model: acceleration is a rate, the change in velocity per second: a = (v − u) ÷ t, where u is the starting velocity and v the final velocity, both in m/s. A family car goes from rest to 90 km/h in 10 seconds. Find its acceleration, then use it to predict its speed after 6 seconds.

1
Formulate: get the units to match
Time is in seconds, so velocity must be in metres per second. 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s, so divide km/h by 3.6.
u = 0 m/s (from rest)
v = 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s
2
Solve: apply the rate
Change in velocity divided by time taken.
a = (25 − 0) ÷ 10 = 2.5 m/s²
The car gains 2.5 m/s every second.
After 6 s: v = 0 + 2.5 × 6 = 15 m/s
3
Interpret and evaluate
On the velocity–time graph the acceleration is the gradient: rise 25 over run 10. 15 m/s × 3.6 = 54 km/h after 6 s, which is believable. The model assumes a constant acceleration; a real car accelerates harder in low gears, so this is an average.
Check: the point (6, 15) lies on the line, because 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 ✓
Model a = 2.5 m/s²  ·  v = 2.5t  ·  after 6 s → 15 m/s (54 km/h)
html.we_do_intro: A family is filling a new rainwater tank with a garden hose. Work through each prompt with a partner, then we check as a class.
html.strategy_section:
★Spot the mistake: acceleration

Before the exit ticket: a student has tried this question and made one mistake. Click the line where the mistake first appears.

A car speeds up from 36 km/h to 90 km/h in 6 seconds. Find its acceleration in m/s².
1 a = (v − u) ÷ t
2 a = (90 − 36) ÷ 6
3 a = 54 ÷ 6
4 a = 9 m/s²

✓ Right: that is where the mistake first appears.

Why: the speeds are still in km/h but the time is in seconds, so the units do not match. Convert first: 36 ÷ 3.6 = 10 m/s and 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s. An acceleration of 9 m/s² would be faster than a Formula One car off the line, which is a sign the model has gone wrong.

Now find the correct acceleration in m/s² (type just the number):

weDo.q: The hose fills a 60 L bucket in 2.5 minutes. What is its flow rate in litres per minute?

fb.150: That is 60 × 2.5. A flow rate is volume ÷ time.

weDo.q: At the same flow rate, how many minutes will it take to fill the 4500 L tank?

fb.108000: You multiplied. Working backwards from a volume to a time means dividing by the flow rate.

weDo.q: Mains water costs $3.30 per kilolitre (1 kL = 1000 L). How much does it cost, in dollars, to fill the 4500 L tank from the mains? (Type just the number.)

fb.14850: The price is per kilolitre: convert 4500 L to kL first.

checkpoint.q: A block of aluminium has a mass of 81 g and a volume of 30 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?

fb.2430: Density is mass ÷ volume, not mass × volume.

checkpoint.q: A cyclist brakes from 12 m/s to a stop in 4 seconds, as shown on the graph. What is the acceleration in m/s²? (Slowing down gives a negative acceleration.)

fb.3: Right size, wrong sign: the cyclist is slowing down, so the acceleration is negative.

practice1.q: A nurse counts 21 heartbeats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
practice1.hint: 15 s is a quarter of a minute, so multiply by 4.

fb.1.4: That is beats per second. Scale up to 60 seconds.

practice1.q: A block of wood has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 400 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?

fb.0.8: That is volume ÷ mass. Density is mass ÷ volume.

practice1.q: A tap flows at 9 L/min. How many litres flow out in 12 minutes?
A trough holds 270 L and fills at 15 L/min. How many minutes does it take to fill?
Convert 54 km/h to metres per second.

fb.194.4: You multiplied by 3.6. To go from km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6.

practice1.q: A car speeds up from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
A bus slows from 30 m/s to a stop in 6 seconds. What is its acceleration in m/s²? (Slowing down is negative.)

fb.5: The bus is slowing down, so the acceleration is negative.

practice1.q: A town of 30 000 people had 450 births last year. What is the birth rate per 1000 people per year?

fb.0.015: That is births per person. Multiply by 1000 to get births per 1000 people.

practice1.q: Gold has a density of 19.3 g/cm³. What is the mass in grams of a 2 cm³ gold nugget?
In a grass fire, the fire front moves 360 m in 12 minutes. What is its rate of spread in metres per minute?

practice2.q: A sports car accelerates from rest to 108 km/h in 12 seconds. What is its acceleration in m/s²?

fb.9: You used km/h with seconds. Convert 108 km/h to m/s first.

practice2.q: A train travelling at 25 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 0.5 m/s² (it loses 0.5 m/s every second). How many seconds does it take to stop?
practice2.hint: Time = change in velocity ÷ rate of change = 25 ÷ 0.5.

fb.12.5: That is 25 × 0.5. Find how many 0.5s fit into 25: divide.

practice2.q: Olive oil has a density of 0.92 g/cm³. What volume, in cm³, does 460 g of oil take up?

fb.423.2: You multiplied. To find volume from mass, divide by the density.

practice2.q: A backyard pool holds 54 000 L. A hose delivers 18 L/min. How many hours will it take to fill the pool?
practice2.hint: 54 000 ÷ 18 = 3000 minutes. Divide by 60 to get hours.

fb.3000: That is the time in minutes. Convert to hours.

practice2.q: A regional city has 48 000 people and a birth rate of 12.5 per 1000 people per year. How many births are expected in a year?
Water costs $2.95 per kL. A shower uses 9 L/min, and Ava has an 8-minute shower every day for 365 days. What is the yearly cost of her shower water, in dollars, to the nearest cent?

fb.77526: The price is per kilolitre: convert litres to kL before multiplying.

practice3.q:
🔥 Simplified classroom model. First Nations rangers plan cool, slow cultural burns using deep knowledge of fuel, wind, temperature and humidity. In this model the rate of spread is directly proportional to wind speed (0–20 km/h) for each fuel, and is halved when relative humidity is above 60%.
Rangers light a cool burn in leaf litter with a wind of 10 km/h and normal humidity. How many minutes will the fire front take to travel 75 m?
practice3.hint: Read the leaf-litter rate from the chart (3 m/min). Time = 75 ÷ 3.

practice3.q: Using the same model: the wind rises to 14 km/h over cured grass (normal humidity). What is the rate of spread in m/min?
practice3.hint: Grass spreads at 15 m/min for 10 km/h, so 1.5 m/min per km/h. Rate = 1.5 × 14.

fb.19: Adding 4 to the rate is not proportional. Find the rate per km/h of wind first (15 ÷ 10).

practice3.q: Early on a cool morning the relative humidity is 75%. A burn in spinifex has a wind of 10 km/h. How far, in metres, does the fire front travel in 40 minutes?
practice3.hint: Humidity above 60% halves the rate: 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 m/min. Distance = 4.5 × 40.

fb.360: Humidity is above 60%, so the rate is halved.

practice3.q: Rangers want a cured-grass burn (normal humidity) to take at least 30 minutes to reach a track 360 m away. According to the model, what is the highest wind speed in km/h they should burn in?
practice3.hint: The rate must be at most 360 ÷ 30 = 12 m/min. Grass: 1.5 m/min per km/h, so wind ≤ 12 ÷ 1.5.

exitProbs.q: A drip irrigation line releases 2.4 L in 15 seconds. What is the flow rate in litres per minute?
exitProbs.hint: 15 s is a quarter of a minute: 2.4 × 4.

exitProbs.q: A car brakes from 72 km/h to a stop in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration in m/s²?

fb.-14.4: Convert 72 km/h to m/s before dividing by the time.
fb.4: The car is slowing down, so the acceleration is negative.

exitProbs.q: First Nations rangers often burn on cool, humid mornings with light wind. Using the idea of rate of spread, explain why these conditions make a burn easier to control. Then name one way this lesson's model is too simple.
exitProbs.hint: Think about what happens to the rate when wind is low and humidity is high, and what else real fires depend on (slope, fuel moisture, fuel load).
